Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama defended himself and his wife Sunday against suggestions that they are insufficiently patriotic. Sen. Barack Obama defended himself and his wife against recent suggestions that they are not patriotic. After a town hall meeting in Lorain, Ohio, a reporter asked Obama about "an attempt by conservatives and Republicans to paint you as unpatriotic." The reporter cited the fact that Obama once failed to put his hand over his heart while singing the national anthem. Obama replied that his choice not to put his hand on his heart is a behavior that "would disqualify about three-quarters of the people who have ever gone to a football game or baseball game." The reporter also noted that the Illinois senator does not wear an American flag lapel pin, has met with former members of the radical anti-Vietnam War group, Weather Underground, and his wife was quoted recently as saying she never felt really proud of the United States until recently. Asked how he would fight the image of being unpatriotic, Obama said, "There's always some nonsense going on in general elections. Right? If it wasn't this, it would be something else. If you recall, first it was my name. Right? That was a problem. And then there was the Muslim e-mail thing and that hasn't worked out so well, and now it's the patriotism thing. "The way I will respond to it is with the truth: that I owe everything I am to this country," he said. The first-term senator from Illinois has been the subject of various debunked rumors since launching his presidential campaign -- allegations that he is a Muslim, that he took his oath of office on a copy of the Quran and that he attended a radical Islamic school while living in Indonesia as a boy. "You will recall that the reason I came to national attention was a speech in which I spoke of my love of this country," said Obama. He and his wife, Michelle, had already explained her comments. "She simply misspoke," he said. "What she was referring to was [that] this was the first time she has been proud of politics in America.  Watch what Michelle Obama said » . "That's true of a lot of people who have been cynical and disenchanted. And she's spoken about how she has been cynical about American politics for a very long time, but she's proud of how people are participating and getting involved in ways that they haven't in a very long time." About not wearing an American flag lapel pin, Obama said Republicans have no lock on patriotism. "A party that presided over a war in which our troops did not get the body armor they needed, or were sending troops over who were untrained because of poor planning, or are not fulfilling the veterans' benefits that these troops need when they come home, or are undermining our Constitution with warrantless wiretaps that are unnecessary? "That is a debate I am very happy to have. We'll see what the American people think is the true definition of patriotism." Obama did not respond to the question about the Weather Underground, a group whose members bombed the U.S. Capitol and the Pentagon during the 1970s. Last week, the New York Sun reported that as an Illinois state senator in 2001, Obama accepted a $200 contribution from William Ayers, a founder of the group who was not convicted for the bombings and now works as a professor at the University of Illinois at Chicago. But the paper said that, in a statement, a spokesman for the Obama campaign, William Burton, said, "Sen. Obama strongly condemns the violent actions of the Weathermen group, as he does all acts of violence ... But he was an 8-year-old child when Ayers and the Weathermen were active, and any attempt to connect Obama with events of almost 40 years ago is ridiculous." Former first lady Sen. Hillary Clinton has said repeatedly that she is a stronger candidate because she has already shown she can withstand conservative attacks. E-mail to a friend .

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — On Sunday, Democratic presidential hopeful Barack Obama rejected claims that he and his wife, Michelle, lacked patriotism.

Following a town hall event in Lorain, Ohio, a journalist asked the Illinois senator about efforts by Republicans and conservatives to portray him as unpatriotic. The reporter pointed to an occasion when Obama did not place his hand over his heart during the national anthem. Obama responded that such a standard “would disqualify about three-quarters of the people who have ever gone to a football game or baseball game.”

The journalist also raised Obama’s decision not to wear a U.S. flag pin, his contact with former members of the radical anti–Vietnam War organization Weather Underground, and Michelle Obama’s recent remark that she had never felt truly proud of the United States until lately.

Asked how he planned to counter that portrayal, Obama said general elections always produce some kind of “nonsense.” He noted that critics had first focused on his name, followed by e-mails falsely suggesting he was Muslim, and were now questioning his patriotism.

His answer, Obama said, would be the truth: “I owe everything I am to this country.”

Since entering the presidential race, the first-term Illinois senator has faced several rumors that have been disproved. Among them were allegations that he is Muslim, that he was sworn into office using a Quran, and that, while living in Indonesia as a child, he attended a radical Islamic school.

Obama said he initially gained nationwide recognition because of a speech in which he expressed his love for America.

He and Michelle Obama had previously addressed her controversial statement. According to Obama, his wife had simply used the wrong words. He said she meant that this was the first time she had felt proud of American politics—not that she had never before been proud of the country. A video of Michelle Obama’s remarks was also available.

Obama added that many Americans had become skeptical and disillusioned. Michelle, he said, had long been cynical about U.S. politics but was encouraged by the way people were taking part and becoming engaged at a level not seen in many years.

Addressing criticism over his refusal to wear an American flag lapel pin, Obama argued that Republicans do not have exclusive ownership of patriotism. He challenged the record of a party that oversaw a war in which troops lacked adequate body armor, deployed some service members without sufficient training because of poor planning, failed to provide returning veterans with the benefits they required, and weakened the Constitution through unnecessary warrantless surveillance.

Obama said he welcomed that debate and was willing to let voters decide what genuine patriotism means.

He did not answer the portion of the question concerning the Weather Underground, whose members bombed both the U.S. Capitol and the Pentagon in the 1970s.

The previous week, the New York Sun reported that Obama, while serving as an Illinois state senator in 2001, received a $200 campaign donation from William Ayers. Ayers helped establish the Weather Underground, was never convicted in connection with its bombings, and later became a professor at the University of Illinois at Chicago.

The newspaper also quoted a statement from Obama campaign spokesman William Burton. Burton said Obama firmly denounced the Weathermen’s violent conduct, just as he condemned every form of violence. He added that Obama had been only 8 years old when Ayers and the organization were active, making any effort to associate him with events from nearly four decades earlier “ridiculous.”

Sen. Hillary Clinton, the former first lady, repeatedly argued that she was the stronger candidate because she had already demonstrated an ability to endure attacks from conservatives.

The original report also included an option to e-mail the story to a friend.
outputs.L3:
Barack Obama defended both himself and his wife, Michelle, against claims by Republicans and conservatives that they were insufficiently patriotic. Critics pointed to several incidents and associations, including Obama’s failure to place his hand over his heart during the national anthem, his decision not to wear an American flag lapel pin, and his alleged ties to former members of the Weather Underground.

Obama rejected these accusations as election-season “nonsense,” comparing them to previously debunked rumors about his name, religion, and personal background. He said he would counter such attacks by emphasizing the truth: that he owed everything he had achieved to the United States and had repeatedly expressed his love for the country in public.

He also defended Michelle over her suggestion that she had only recently felt truly proud of the United States. Obama said she had simply misspoken and that her comment did not reflect any lack of patriotism or appreciation for the country.
outputs.L4:
Barack Obama responded to Republican and conservative accusations that he and his wife, Michelle, were insufficiently patriotic, dismissing the charges as politically motivated efforts to damage his presidential campaign. He addressed several incidents that critics had cited as evidence, including photographs of him standing without his hand over his heart, his decision at times not to wear an American flag pin, questions about his associations, and remarks by Michelle Obama about being proud of her country.

Obama explained that isolated gestures or images did not accurately reflect his beliefs. He noted that the photograph involving his hand position was taken during the national anthem rather than the Pledge of Allegiance and rejected the idea that wearing a flag pin was the sole measure of patriotism. He argued that love of country should instead be demonstrated through a person’s actions, public service, and commitment to improving the lives of fellow Americans.

He also defended Michelle’s comments, saying they had been taken out of context. Her remarks, he maintained, expressed enthusiasm about the unprecedented level of public engagement surrounding the campaign rather than a lack of pride in the United States. More broadly, Obama said that criticism based on controversial people he had encountered or known did not fairly represent his own views or record.

Pointing to his life and career, Obama emphasized that the opportunities he had received were possible only in America. His education, work as a community organizer, public service, and rise to national prominence reflected both his gratitude to the country and his belief in its promise. He stressed that he owed everything he had achieved to the United States and remained deeply committed to its ideals.

Obama characterized the accusations as baseless campaign tactics similar to earlier rumors and attacks that had already been disproved. Rather than engaging with substantive questions about policy or leadership, he argued, his opponents were attempting to create doubts about his identity and loyalty. He framed the controversy as another unsuccessful effort to undermine his candidacy by questioning his patriotism instead of debating his plans for the country.

As the 44th president of the United States, Obama became a prominent Democratic leader and the first African American to hold the presidency. His administration focused on issues such as healthcare reform, economic recovery, climate policy, and international cooperation. Years after leaving office, Barack Obama remains an influential figure in Democratic politics, often supporting candidates and encouraging voter participation.
